title: Galaxies and the universe
introduction: You already know our solar system belongs to the Milky Way. But does everything belong to that one galaxy?
We will look beyond our home galaxy and meet other galaxies.
Along the way, we will learn what different space pictures can really tell us.

steps.title: Remember our place
paragraphs: Earth travels around the Sun.
Our solar system includes the Sun, planets, moons, and smaller objects.
This whole family belongs to the Milky Way.
The Milky Way contains many stars beyond our Sun.
Knowing our home helps us ask a bigger question: what lies outside it?
steps.invitation: Follow our place from Earth to the universe.
steps.glaux: A home can belong to a much wider neighborhood.

steps.title: What fills a galaxy?
paragraphs: A galaxy is a huge gathering of stars and other material.
Many stars have planets.
Between stars, there is gas and dust.
Gas is material like air, often spread very thinly.
Space dust means tiny grains, not household dirt.
We see much of this material through the light it gives off, blocks, or reflects.
steps.invitation: Choose stars, gas or dust to explore the model.

steps.title: Why is it one galaxy?
paragraphs: Gravity is the pull that objects have on one another.
It helps hold stars and other material together within a galaxy.
The Milky Way is more than a picture of crowded lights.
It is a connected system.
Our solar system is one small part of it, not a second galaxy.
steps.invitation: Look at how our small solar system belongs to a galaxy.

steps.title: Beyond our Milky Way
paragraphs: Astronomers use telescopes to observe galaxies outside our own.
Each is a separate gathering of stars and other material.
A distant galaxy may look like one soft patch.
That does not mean it is one star.
A telescope can reveal more of the galaxy's shape and detail.
steps.invitation: Explore an observed field containing many galaxies.
steps.glaux: One faint patch may contain countless individual lights.

steps.title: Meet Andromeda
paragraphs: Andromeda is another galaxy, separate from the Milky Way.
In a wide picture, its many stars blend into a gentle glow.
Darker patches mark dust that blocks some starlight.
This is a view of Andromeda from our part of space.
It is not an outside photograph of our Milky Way.
steps.invitation: Look for the bright middle and dark dust lanes.

steps.title: Different shapes
paragraphs: Galaxies do not all look alike.
Some have curving arms and are called spiral galaxies.
Others look smooth and rounded or oval. These are called elliptical galaxies.
Some have less regular shapes. A galaxy can also look different from another viewing angle.
These descriptions help us compare appearances; they do not put every galaxy into a perfect box.
steps.invitation: Compare the spiral and the smooth oval. Equal panels do not mean equal sizes.

steps.title: What does a telescope picture show?
paragraphs: A telescope records light coming from real objects.
Scientists may join several observations into one image.
They may also choose colours to reveal details.
Such an image still uses real measurements.
Yet its colours may differ from what our eyes would see.
A telescope picture is evidence, not always an ordinary snapshot.
steps.invitation: Choose a feature to compare the observation and diagram.

steps.title: What does a drawing show?
paragraphs: You have already compared two views of our Milky Way. Now ask how each picture was made.
A diagram simplifies something to explain a relationship.
An artist's reconstruction pictures a scene we cannot photograph directly. Observations guide it, but some details may be uncertain.
We cannot photograph our whole Milky Way from far outside it. An outside drawing helps explain its structure without becoming a photograph.
steps.invitation: Compare the observation with an evidence-guided outside view.
steps.glaux: Ask what a picture knows, and what it only suggests.

steps.title: What is the universe?
paragraphs: The Milky Way is one galaxy.
Andromeda is another.
Both belong to the universe.
The universe means all space and everything in it.
That includes stars, galaxies, and the space between them.
A picture showing several galaxies still shows only a tiny portion of this larger whole.
steps.invitation: Follow the relationships again, now including other galaxies.

steps.title: Does our view have an edge?
paragraphs: Light needs time to travel. Some regions are too far away for their light to have reached us.
Astronomers call the region from which light has had time to reach us the observable universe.
That limit does not mean the whole universe ends there. We do not know its full extent.
A limit to our view is not a solid wall in space. There is still much to discover.
steps.invitation: Explore what a picture can and cannot tell us.

recap.title: Three things to keep
paragraphs: Our solar system lies in the Milky Way, one of many galaxies.
The universe includes all space and everything in it.
Telescope images, diagrams and reconstructions provide different kinds of information.
recap.glaux: Our home is one part of a much wider sky.

glossary.definition: Our Sun and the objects linked to it by gravity.
glossary.example: Earth and its Moon are part of our solar system.

glossary.definition: A vast gathering of stars, gas and dust, held together by gravity.
glossary.example: The Milky Way is a galaxy.

glossary.definition: Material that spreads to fill its surroundings.
glossary.example: Air is a gas; space also has very thin gas.

glossary.definition: Very small solid grains scattered through space.
glossary.example: Dust can block light from stars.

glossary.definition: The pull between objects with mass.
glossary.example: Gravity keeps Earth moving around the Sun.

glossary.definition: Galaxies that look mostly smooth and round or oval.
glossary.example: IC 2006 has a smooth, roughly oval appearance.

glossary.definition: An instrument that collects light to help us study distant objects.
glossary.example: A telescope records light coming from Andromeda.

glossary.definition: A simplified drawing that explains a relationship.
glossary.example: A relationship map shows our solar system within the Milky Way.

glossary.definition: An evidence-guided picture of a view we cannot photograph directly.
glossary.example: An artist pictures our Milky Way from outside.

glossary.definition: All space and everything in it.
glossary.example: The Milky Way and Andromeda both belong to the universe.

glossary.definition: The region from which light has had time to reach us.
glossary.example: Its observational limit is not a wall around the whole universe.

choice.prompt: Which path moves from our familiar home toward the widest idea?
choice.hint: A solar system belongs inside a galaxy, not the other way around.
choice.explanation: Earth belongs to our solar system. Our solar system lies inside the Milky Way. Our galaxy belongs to the universe.

options.text: Earth → solar system → Milky Way → universe
options.feedback: You kept each smaller home inside the wider one.

options.text: Earth → Milky Way → solar system → universe
options.feedback: You found the groups. Try placing our solar system inside the Milky Way.

options.text: Earth → solar system → universe → Milky Way
options.feedback: The Milky Way belongs inside the universe. Try those last two again.
Earth travels around the Sun, not inside it. Andromeda is a different galaxy.

evidence.prompt: What can these pictures tell us?
evidence.hint: Look at how each picture was made and what its caption says.

questions.prompt: The two galaxy pictures used equal-sized panels. Does that prove equal galaxy sizes?

options.text: Yes, the galaxies must be equally large.
options.feedback: The panels belong to the page layout. They do not compare the galaxies' real sizes.

options.text: No, the panels do not compare real sizes.
options.feedback: You separated the picture's size from the galaxy's size.

questions.prompt: Can a telescope observation use colours different from what our eyes would see?

options.text: Yes, colours can help display measured light.
options.feedback: Real observations can use processed colours to reveal details.

options.text: No, every observation must match unaided-eye vision.
options.feedback: Measured light can be combined and assigned display colours. It is still an observation.

questions.prompt: Does the Gaia reconstruction mean a camera photographed our entire galaxy from outside?

options.text: Yes, it is a direct outside photograph.
options.feedback: Gaia collected measurements. An artist used evidence to picture this outside view.

options.text: No, measurements guide an artist's reconstruction.
options.feedback: You recognised a view built from evidence, rather than an outside photograph.
